propositions.text: Appeal raises standing and abuse of process issues involving Aboriginal community, logging company, and provincial government.
propositions.quote: This appeal raises issues of standing and abuse of process in the context of relations between members of an Aboriginal community, a logging company, and a provincial government.

propositions.text: Crown granted licences to logging company to harvest timber on Fort Nelson First Nation territory.
propositions.quote: After the Crown had granted licences to a logging company to harvest timber in two areas on the territory of the Fort Nelson First Nation (“FNFN”) in British Columbia

propositions.text: Individuals from FNFN erected a camp blocking company's access to logging sites.
propositions.quote: a number of individuals from that First Nation erected a camp that, in effect, blocked the company’s access to the logging sites.

propositions.text: Company sued Aboriginal community members who defended by alleging licences were void due to breach of constitutional duty to consult and treaty rights violation.
propositions.quote: The company brought a tort action against these members of the Aboriginal community, who argued in their defence that the licences were void because they had been issued in breach of the constitutional duty to consult and because they violated the community members’ treaty rights.

paragraphs.summary: Court states appeal involves standing and abuse of process issues about Aboriginal community blocking logging company access, alleging licences void.

propositions.text: Courts below held Behns lacked standing to assert collective rights; only community could raise such rights.
propositions.quote: The courts below held that the individual members of the Aboriginal community (the “Behns”) did not have standing to assert collective rights in their defence; only the community could raise such rights.

propositions.text: Courts below concluded challenge to licence validity was collateral attack or abuse of process as Behns failed to challenge validity when issued.
propositions.quote: The courts below also concluded that such a challenge to the validity of the licences amounted to a collateral attack or an abuse of process, as the Behns had failed to challenge the validity of the licences when they were issued.

paragraphs.summary: Courts below found Behns lacked standing to assert collective rights and that challenging licences was abuse of process.

propositions.text: Court must decide if individual Aboriginal members can raise breach of Aboriginal and treaty rights as defence and in what circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Court is asked to consider in this appeal whether an individual member or group of members of an Aboriginal community can raise a breach of Aboriginal and treaty rights as a defence to a tort action and, if so, in what circumstances.

propositions.text: Court must also decide if abuse of process doctrine applies in this case as standing question is not determinative.
propositions.quote: But, as this question of standing is not determinative for the purposes of this appeal, the Court must also decide whether the doctrine of abuse of process applies in this case.

paragraphs.summary: Court will decide if individual Aboriginal members can raise breach of rights as defence and if abuse of process applies.

propositions.text: Court would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court states it would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Facts taken from pleadings as appeal is from motion to strike pleadings.
propositions.quote: As this is an appeal from a decision on a motion to strike pleadings, the following facts are taken from the pleadings.

propositions.text: Behns, except one, are members of Fort Nelson First Nation, a band under Indian Act.
propositions.quote: The Behns are, with one exception, members of the FNFN, a “band” within the meaning of the Indian Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-5 .

propositions.text: FNFN is party to Treaty No. 8 covering parts of Alberta, BC, Saskatchewan, Northwest Territories.
propositions.quote: The FNFN is a party to Treaty No. 8 of 1899, which covers an area comprising parts of Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories.

propositions.text: Behns allege they traditionally hunted and trapped on part of FNFN territory allocated to their family.
propositions.quote: The Behns allege that they have traditionally hunted and trapped on a part of the FNFN’s territory that has historically been allocated to their family.

paragraphs.summary: Court states facts from pleadings: Behns mostly FNFN members, treaty party, allege traditional hunting on family territory.

propositions.text: Moulton Contracting Ltd. is BC company granted two timber sale licences and road permit by BC Ministry of Forests on June 27, 2006.
propositions.quote: Moulton Contracting Ltd. (“Moulton”) is a company incorporated pursuant to the laws of British Columbia. On June 27, 2006, the British Columbia Ministry of Forests (“MOF”) granted Moulton two timber sale licences and a road permit (the “Authorizations”) pursuant to the Forest Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 157.

propositions.text: Authorizations allowed Moulton to harvest timber on two parcels within FNFN territory, within Behn family trapline.
propositions.quote: These Authorizations entitled Moulton to harvest timber on two parcels of land within the FNFN’s territory, both of which are within the Behn family trapline.

propositions.text: FNFN manages territory by allocating traplines to families headed by a headman.
propositions.quote: The Behns stated in their Amended Statement of Defence that the FNFN manages its territory by allocating parts of it (called traplines) to specific families: While the rights provided for in the Treaty # 8 extended throughout the tract described in the treaty, most of the aboriginal people comprising the Fort Nelson First Nation traditionally ordered themselves so that the rights to hunt and trap set out in Treaty 8 were exercised in tracts of land associated with different extended families. These extended families were headed by a headman.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Moulton got licences to harvest timber on FNFN land within Behn trapline; FNFN allocates traplines to families.

propositions.text: MOF contacted FNFN and individual trappers including George Behn in 2004 about forest development plan amendments and harvesting blocks.
propositions.quote: Before granting the Authorizations, the MOF had contacted representatives of the FNFN and individual trappers, including George Behn, the headman of the Behn family, in developing and amending its forest development plan (“FDP”). The MOF contacted the FNFN in August 2004 and individual trappers, including Mr. Behn, in September 2004 to notify them that additional harvesting blocks were being proposed.

propositions.text: Trappers invited to provide concerns or comments by October 20, 2004; MOF met FNFN in November 2004 to discuss consultation and funding.
propositions.quote: The trappers it contacted were invited to advise it of any concerns they had or provide it with comments by October 20, 2004. MOF officials met a representative of the FNFN in November 2004 to discuss consultation on the proposed amendment to the FDP. The issue of funding to enable the FNFN to provide information to the MOF was discussed at that meeting. Funding was ultimately refused.

propositions.text: MOF informed FNFN in January 2005 about archaeological impact assessments; assessments done August 2005 and delivered to FNFN; further meeting in September 2005.
propositions.quote: On January 31, 2005, the MOF wrote to the FNFN to advise it that archaeological impact assessments would be conducted for certain areas proposed for harvesting in the amendment to the FDP. Two archaeological impact assessments were completed in August 2005, and copies of them were delivered to the FNFN. The MOF and the FNFN met again on September 21, 2005 to discuss the proposed amendment further.

paragraphs.summary: Court details MOF's consultations with FNFN and trappers including Behn about forest plan and assessments.

propositions.text: MOF approved FDP amendment and put timber sale licences up for sale June 2, 2006.
propositions.quote: The MOF approved the amendment to the FDP. On June 2, 2006, it put the two timber sale licences relevant to this appeal up for sale.

propositions.text: MOF granted Authorizations to Moulton and notified George Behn on June 28 and July 17, 2006 about licences and harvesting start date.
propositions.quote: After granting the Authorizations to Moulton, the MOF wrote to George Behn on June 28, 2006, to advise him that Moulton had been awarded licences to harvest timber within his trapping area. In that letter, George Behn was advised to contact Moulton directly to confirm the date its harvesting operations were to commence. The MOF again wrote to Mr. Behn on July 17, 2006, to advise him that the operations would begin on August 1, 2006.

propositions.text: George Behn wrote to MOF on August 31, 2006 requesting cancellation of Authorizations and seeking consultation; no copy sent to Moulton.
propositions.quote: On August 31, 2006, George Behn wrote to the MOF, requesting that the Authorizations granted to Moulton be cancelled and seeking consultation. No copy of this letter was sent to Moulton.

paragraphs.summary: Court states MOF approved licences, notified Behn, who later requested cancellation and consultation but did not notify Moulton.

propositions.text: Moulton began moving equipment to first site September 19-22, 2006.
propositions.quote: Between September 19 and September 22, 2006, Moulton started moving its equipment to one of the two sites to which the Authorizations applied.

propositions.text: MOF notified Moulton of potential problem with George Behn on September 25, 2006 and requested moving operations to second site.
propositions.quote: On September 25, 2006, the MOF notified Moulton that there was a potential problem with George Behn. The MOF requested that Moulton move its operations to the second site.

propositions.text: Moulton replied it could not move because of commitments to mill to deliver timber from first site.
propositions.quote: Moulton replied that it could not do so because it had commitments to a mill to deliver timber from the first site.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Moulton moved equipment to first site; MOF asked to move due to Behn issue; Moulton refused due to mill commitments.

propositions.text: In early October 2006, Behns erected camp blocking access road to timber harvesting sites authorized to Moulton.
propositions.quote: In early October 2006, the Behns erected a camp on the access road leading to the parcels of land to which the Authorizations applied. The camp blocked access to the land where Moulton was authorized to harvest timber.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Behns erected camp blocking access to Moulton's authorized timber sites in early October 2006.

propositions.text: Moulton sued Behns, Chief Logan, FNFN, and Crown for damages for interference with contractual relations on November 23, 2006.
propositions.quote: On November 23, 2006, Moulton filed a statement of claim in the British Columbia Supreme Court against the Behns, Chief Logan on behalf of herself and the FNFN, and the Crown. Moulton claimed damages from the Behns for interference with contractual relations.

propositions.text: Behns denied unlawful conduct and alleged Authorizations were illegal due to Crown's failure to consult and treaty rights infringement.
propositions.quote: In their statement of defence, the Behns denied that their conduct was unlawful. They alleged that the Authorizations were illegal for two reasons. First, the Crown had failed to fulfil its duty to consult in issuing the Authorizations. Second, the Authorizations infringed their hunting and trapping rights under Treaty No. 8.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Moulton sued Behns for interference; Behns denied unlawfulness and alleged licences illegal due to duty to consult breach and treaty rights infringement.

propositions.text: Moulton applied to strike parts of Behns' defence as disclosing no reasonable defence or abuse of process under Supreme Court Rules.
propositions.quote: Moulton applied under Rule 19(24) of the Supreme Court Rules, B.C. Reg. 221/90 [repealed] (now Rule 9-5(1), Supreme Court Civil Rules, B.C. Reg. 168/2009), to have a number of paragraphs struck out of the Behns’ statement of defence on the ground (1) that it was plain and obvious that they did not disclose a reasonable defence, or (2) that the relief being sought in them constituted an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Moulton sought to strike paragraphs alleging Authorizations invalid due to breach of duty to consult and treaty rights and that acts were not illegal or tortious.
propositions.quote: In substance, the paragraphs Moulton sought to have struck related to the Behns’ allegations that the Authorizations were invalid because they had been issued in breach of the Crown’s duty to consult and because they violated the Behns’ treaty rights, and to their allegations that their acts were neither illegal nor tortious.

propositions.text: Crown supported Moulton's application and argued Behns lacked standing to raise breach of duty to consult or treaty rights; only FNFN had standing.
propositions.quote: The Crown supported Moulton’s application and further submitted that the Behns lacked standing to raise a breach of the duty to consult or of treaty rights, as only the FNFN had such standing.

paragraphs.summary: Moulton applied to strike Behns' defence alleging invalid licences and lack of illegality; Crown supported, arguing Behns lacked standing.

propositions.text: Hinkson J. held Behns lacked standing to raise defences on duty to consult and treaty rights as these are collective rights.
propositions.quote: Hinkson J. held that the Behns lacked standing to raise the defences pertaining to the duty to consult and treaty rights. He stated that although Aboriginal and treaty rights are exercised by individuals, they are collective in nature.

propositions.text: Collective rights not possessed by individuals; individuals can assert only if authorized by collective; FNFN had not authorized Behns.
propositions.quote: As a result, they are not possessed by nor do they reside with individuals. He mentioned that collective rights can be asserted by individuals only if the individuals are authorized to do so by the collective. Hinkson J. found that the FNFN had not authorized the Behns to assert these rights.

paragraphs.summary: Hinkson J. found Behns lacked standing to raise collective rights defences without FNFN authorization.

propositions.text: Hinkson J. held paragraphs alleging invalid Authorizations struck as abuse of process; Behns should have applied for judicial review.
propositions.quote: Hinkson J. also held that the impugned paragraphs in which the Behns submitted that the Authorizations were invalid had to be struck out as an abuse of process under Rule 19(24) of the Supreme Court Rules. He reasoned that the Behns could not be permitted to introduce the subject matter of the invalidity of the Authorizations now in their statement of defence, as they should instead have applied for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Hinkson J. struck paragraphs alleging invalid Authorizations as abuse of process; Behns should have sought judicial review.

propositions.text: Trial proceeded on surviving paragraphs from September to November 2011; judgment reserved pending this Court's decision.
propositions.quote: It should be noted that the trial then proceeded from September to November 2011 in the British Columbia Supreme Court on the basis of the paragraphs that had survived the motion to strike. The trial judge has reserved his judgment until this Court disposes of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Trial proceeded on surviving pleadings; judgment reserved pending Supreme Court decision.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed Behns lacked standing to assert duty to consult breach and collective rights infringement without FNFN authorization.
propositions.quote: Saunders J.A., writing for the Court of Appeal, agreed with Hinkson J. that the Behns lacked standing to assert that the duty to consult owed to the FNFN had not been met and that collective rights had been infringed by the issuance of the Authorizations.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal stated attack on non-Aboriginal party's rights based on treaty requires collective authorization; Behns had none.
propositions.quote: She said, at para. 39, that “an attack on a non-Aboriginal party’s rights, on the basis of treaty or constitutional propositions, requires authorization by the collective in whom the treaty and constitutional rights inhere”. In this case, the Behns had received no such authorization by the FNFN.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal did not suggest collective rights could never provide defence to individual Aboriginal members.
propositions.quote: Saunders J.A. was careful to point out that she was not suggesting that collective rights could never provide a defence to individual members of an Aboriginal community.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal agreed Behns lacked standing without FNFN authorization but did not rule out collective rights defence for individuals.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal concluded Behns' defences were impermissible collateral attack on Authorizations; FNFN could challenge Authorizations legally.
propositions.quote: Saunders J.A. also concluded that the defences raised by the Behns constituted an impermissible collateral attack upon the Authorizations granted to Moulton. She added that this conclusion was not incompatible with the proper administration of justice, since the FNFN, as a collective, had the capacity to challenge the Authorizations through a number of legal avenues.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal upheld abuse of process conclusion against Behns' defences.
propositions.quote: She therefore upheld Hinkson J.’s conclusion that the impugned defences constituted an abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found Behns' defences were collateral attack and abuse of process; FNFN could challenge Authorizations.

propositions.text: Three issues: can Behns assert breach of duty to consult; can treaty rights be invoked by individuals; does abuse of process apply?
propositions.quote: Three issues must be addressed in this appeal. First, can the Behns, as individual members of an Aboriginal community, assert a breach of the duty to consult? This issue raises the question to whom the Crown owes a duty to consult. Second, can treaty rights be invoked by individual members of an Aboriginal community? These two issues relate to standing.

propositions.text: Third issue is whether challenging validity of Authorizations now is abuse of process given failure to act earlier despite objections.
propositions.quote: The third issue relates to abuse of process. Does it amount to an abuse of process for the Behns to challenge the validity of the Authorizations now that they are being sued by Moulton after having failed to take legal action when the Authorizations were first issued even though they objected to their validity at the time?

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies three issues: standing to assert duty to consult breach, treaty rights invocation, and abuse of process.

propositions.text: Does it amount to an abuse of process for the Behns to challenge the validity of the Authorizations now?
propositions.quote: Does it amount to an abuse of process for the Behns to challenge the validity of the Authorizations now that they are being sued by Moulton after having failed to take legal action when the Authorizations were first issued even though they objected to their validity at the time?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether it is abuse of process for the Behns to now challenge the Authorizations' validity after previously objecting but not suing.

propositions.text: Behns argue Court of Appeal erred in holding they lacked standing and that challenging Authorizations was collateral attack.
propositions.quote: The Behns submit that the Court of Appeal erred in holding that they lacked standing to assert defences based on treaty rights and that challenging the validity of the Authorizations constituted an impermissible collateral attack.

propositions.text: Behns contend standing principles apply to claims, not defences; thus do not apply here as they are defending.
propositions.quote: The Behns contend that the principles related to standing apply to the assertion of a claim, not of a defence. As a result, they do not apply in this case, since the Behns are simply defending against an action.

propositions.text: Alternatively, Behns assert they have standing as FNFN members with substantial and direct interest in Treaty No. 8 rights.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Behns assert that they have standing because, as members of the FNFN, they have a substantial and direct interest in their rights under Treaty No. 8.

paragraphs.summary: Behns argue Court of Appeal erred on standing and collateral attack; say standing applies to claims not defences; assert standing as FNFN members.

propositions.text: The Behns argue their defences do not constitute a collateral attack as they are not parties to the Authorizations, relying on Garland v. Consumers’ Gas Co.
propositions.quote: the Behns argue, relying on Garland v. Consumers’ Gas Co., 2004 SCC 25, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 629, that the defences they assert do not constitute a collateral attack, since they are not parties to the Authorizations.

propositions.text: Alternatively, if the defences are a collateral attack, it is permissible because legislature did not intend lawfulness of Authorizations to be questioned only by judicial review.
propositions.quote: Alternatively, they submit that, if the impugned paragraphs do constitute a collateral attack, the attack is permissible, because the legislature did not intend that any attempt to question the lawfulness of the Authorizations could be made only by applying for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The Behns argue their defences are not a collateral attack or are permissible if so, relying on Garland and legislative intent.

propositions.text: The Behns submit that the rule of law principle will be violated if they cannot assert their defences, as lawfulness of their conduct depends on lawfulness of Authorizations.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Behns submit that the principle of the rule of law will be violated if they cannot assert their defences. They contend that whether their conduct was lawful cannot be determined without also addressing the lawfulness of the Authorizations.

paragraphs.summary: The Behns submit rule of law is violated if they cannot assert defences tied to lawfulness of Authorizations.

propositions.text: Moulton argues Behns lack standing to raise Aboriginal or treaty rights defence; only FNFN can assert such claims.
propositions.quote: Moulton responds that the Behns have no standing to raise a defence based on Aboriginal or treaty rights, because only the FNFN, as the collective, can assert a claim that these rights have been infringed.

propositions.text: Moulton contends Crown’s duty to consult is owed to collective, not individual members.
propositions.quote: Moulton also contends that the Crown’s duty to consult is owed to the collective, not to individual members of the collective.

propositions.text: Moulton says Behns rely on affirmative defence requiring order declaring Authorizations invalid, not mere dismissal of action.
propositions.quote: Responding to the Behns’ submission that they have standing because they are only seeking the dismissal of the action, Moulton submits that they are relying on an affirmative defence that requires an order declaring the Authorizations to be invalid.

propositions.text: Moulton argues Behns’ blockade activity is not a right protected under Treaty No. 8.
propositions.quote: Moulton adds that the activity for which the Behns are now being sued — erecting and participating in a blockade — is not a right protected under Treaty No. 8.

propositions.text: Moulton submits Behns’ challenge to Authorizations now is collateral attack; they should have applied for judicial review earlier.
propositions.quote: Finally, since the Behns could have challenged the legality of the Authorizations by applying for judicial review when they were issued, Moulton submits that it amounts to a collateral attack for the Behns to challenge their validity now as a defence to a tort claim.

paragraphs.summary: Moulton argues Behns lack standing, their defence requires invalidation order, blockade not protected right, and challenge is impermissible collateral attack.

propositions.text: Crown says Aboriginal and treaty rights claims must be brought by or on behalf of Aboriginal community due to collective nature.
propositions.quote: According to the Crown, the collective nature of Aboriginal and treaty rights means that claims in relation to such rights must be brought by, or on behalf of, the Aboriginal community.

propositions.text: Crown recognizes Behns’ interest but says issue concerns blockade defence, not hunting or trapping rights.
propositions.quote: Although the Crown recognizes the Behns’ interest in their treaty rights, it submits that their position on this issue disregards two factors: (1) the issue arising in the litigation concerns a defence to a claim related to a blockade, not to the exercise of hunting or trapping rights;

propositions.text: Crown notes FNFN is party and represents community in proceedings.
propositions.quote: and (2) the FNFN is named as a party to the proceedings and therefore represents the community in them.

propositions.text: Crown submits substantial interest in treaty right does not entitle individual to bring treaty rights claim or defence.
propositions.quote: The Crown further submits that having a substantial and direct interest in a treaty right does not entitle an individual to bring a treaty rights claim or defence.

paragraphs.summary: Crown argues treaty rights claims must be by community; Behns’ interest noted but issue is blockade defence; FNFN represents community; individual interest insufficient.

propositions.text: Crown submits impugned defences challenge validity of Authorizations, so are collateral attack if claimant not content to let decision stand.
propositions.quote: On whether the impugned paragraphs constitute an impermissible collateral attack, the Crown submits that the question is whether the claimant is content to let the government’s decision stand. In the instant case, the impugned defences raise an unequivocal challenge to the validity and legal force of the Authorizations.

propositions.text: Crown submits Behns could have challenged Authorizations by judicial review instead of blockading road.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Crown submits that the Behns could have challenged the validity of the Authorizations by applying for judicial review instead of blockading a road.

paragraphs.summary: Crown argues defences challenge Authorizations’ validity and Behns should have sought judicial review, not blockade.

propositions.text: Whether the Behns can assert the duty to consult on their own as a defence to Moulton’s claim.
propositions.quote: The question that arises with respect to this particular defence is whether the Behns can assert the duty to consult on their own in the first place.

paragraphs.summary: Court poses issue whether Behns can assert duty to consult on their own as defence.

propositions.text: Haida Nation confirms Crown’s duty to consult Aboriginal peoples before final claims resolution is essential to reconciliation under s. 35.
propositions.quote: In Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 511, this Court confirmed that the Crown has a duty to consult Aboriginal peoples and explained the scope of application of that duty in respect of Aboriginal rights, stating that “consultation and accommodation before final claims resolution, while challenging, is not impossible, and indeed is an essential corollary to the honourable process of reconciliation that s. 35 [of the Constitution Act, 1982 ] demands”: para. 38.

propositions.text: Mikisew Cree holds duty to consult applies in treaty rights context.
propositions.quote: In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 2005 SCC 69, [2005] 3 S.C.R. 388, the Court held that the duty to consult applies in the context of treaty rights: paras. 32-34.

propositions.text: Crown cannot contract out of duty to consult Aboriginal peoples, applies independently of parties’ intention.
propositions.quote: The Crown cannot in a treaty contract out of its duty to consult Aboriginal peoples, as this duty “applies independently of the expressed or implied intention of the parties”: Beckman v. Little Salmon/Carmacks First Nation, 2010 SCC 53, [2010] 3 S.C.R. 103, at para. 61.

paragraphs.summary: Prior cases confirm Crown’s constitutional duty to consult Aboriginal peoples, including treaty rights, cannot be contracted out.

propositions.text: Duty to consult is legal and constitutional, grounded in honour of the Crown, supporting reconciliation process.
propositions.quote: The duty to consult is both a legal and a constitutional duty: Haida Nation, at para. 10; R. v. Kapp, 2008 SCC 41, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 483, at para. 6; see also J. Woodward, Native Law, vol. 1 (loose-leaf), at p. 5-38. This duty is grounded in the honour of the Crown: Haida Nation, Beckman, at para. 38; Kapp, at para. 6. As Binnie J. said in Beckman, at para. 44, “[t]he concept of the duty to consult is a valuable adjunct to the honour of the Crown, but it plays a supporting role, and should not be viewed independently from its purpose.” The duty to consult is part of the process for achieving “the reconciliation of the pre-existence of aboriginal societies with the sovereignty of the Crown”: Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1010, at para. 186, quoting R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507, at para. 31; Haida Nation, at para. 17; see also D. G. Newman, The Duty to Consult: New Relationships with Aboriginal Peoples (2009).

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult is legal and constitutional, grounded in honour of Crown, supporting reconciliation of Aboriginal societies and Crown sovereignty.

propositions.text: Duty to consult triggered when Crown knows of potential Aboriginal right and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it.
propositions.quote: The duty to consult is triggered “when the Crown has knowledge, real or constructive, of the potential existence of the Aboriginal right or title and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it”: Haida Nation, at para. 35.

propositions.text: Duty content varies on spectrum; requires good faith by Crown and Aboriginal peoples; no veto or agreement required.
propositions.quote: The content of the duty varies depending on the context, as it lies on a spectrum of different actions to be taken by the Crown: Haida Nation, at para. 43. An important component of the duty to consult is a requirement that good faith be shown by both the Crown and the Aboriginal people in question: Haida Nation, at para. 42. Both parties must take a reasonable and fair approach in their dealings. The duty does not require that an agreement be reached, nor does it give Aboriginal peoples a veto: Taku River Tlingit First Nation v. British Columbia (Project Assessment Director), 2004 SCC 74, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 550, at paras. 2 and 22; Haida Nation, at para. 48.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult triggers on Crown’s knowledge of potential Aboriginal right and requires good faith, no veto or agreement needed.

propositions.text: Duty to consult protects collective Aboriginal rights and is owed to Aboriginal group holding s. 35 rights.
propositions.quote: The duty to consult exists to protect the collective rights of Aboriginal peoples. For this reason, it is owed to the Aboriginal group that holds the s. 35 rights, which are collective in nature: Beckman, at para. 35; Woodward, at p. 5-55.

propositions.text: Aboriginal group can authorize individual or organization to represent it for asserting s. 35 rights.
propositions.quote: But an Aboriginal group can authorize an individual or an organization to represent it for the purpose of asserting its s. 35 rights: see, e.g., Komoyue Heritage Society v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2006 BCSC 1517, 55 Admin. L.R. (4th) 236.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult protects collective rights owed to Aboriginal group, which can authorize individuals to represent it.

propositions.text: No pleadings show FNFN authorized Behns to represent it in contesting Authorizations’ legality.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, it does not appear from the pleadings that the FNFN authorized George Behn or any other person to represent it for the purpose of contesting the legality of the Authorizations.

propositions.text: FNFN was party below and an intervener here; Moulton alleged FNFN conspired to block access.
propositions.quote: As a matter of fact, the FNFN was a party in the proceedings in the courts below, because Moulton was arguing that it had combined or conspired with others to block access to Moulton’s logging sites. The FNFN is also an intervener in this Court.

propositions.text: Without authorization allegation, Behns cannot assert breach of duty to consult on their own; pleadings provide no basis for such claim here.
propositions.quote: But, given the absence of an allegation of an authorization from the FNFN, in the circumstances of this case, the Behns cannot assert a breach of the duty to consult on their own, as that duty is owed to the Aboriginal community, the FNFN. Even if it were assumed that such a claim by individuals is possible, the allegations in the pleadings provide no basis for one in the context of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no FNFN authorization for Behns; thus Behns cannot assert duty to consult breach on their own here.

propositions.text: Behns challenge Authorizations’ legality as breaching their Treaty No. 8 hunting and trapping rights, but definitive ruling premature.
propositions.quote: The Behns also challenge the legality of the Authorizations on the basis that they breach their rights to hunt and trap under Treaty No. 8. This is an important issue, but a definitive pronouncement in this regard cannot be made in the circumstances of this case.

propositions.text: Court cautions against definitive ruling at this stage of proceedings and law development.
propositions.quote: I would caution against doing so at this stage of the proceedings and of the development of the law.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Behns’ Treaty No. 8 rights challenge but cautions against definitive ruling now.

propositions.text: Crown argues treaty rights claims must be brought by or on behalf of Aboriginal community due to collective nature.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that claims in relation to treaty rights must be brought by, or on behalf of, the Aboriginal community.

propositions.text: Court finds Crown’s general proposition too narrow; some rights have individual aspects exercisable by members.
propositions.quote: This general proposition is too narrow. It is true that Aboriginal and treaty rights are collective in nature: see R. v. Sparrow... However, certain rights... are nonetheless exercised by individual members or assigned to them.

propositions.text: Individual members may have vested interest and may assert certain Aboriginal or treaty rights in appropriate circumstances.
propositions.quote: Individual members of a community may have a vested interest in the protection of these rights. It may well be that, in appropriate circumstances, individual members can assert certain Aboriginal or treaty rights, as some of the interveners have proposed.

paragraphs.summary: Crown argues treaty rights claims must be by community; court finds some rights have individual aspects and members may assert rights.

propositions.text: Interveners propose classifying Aboriginal and treaty rights into three types: exclusively collective, mixed, and predominantly individual.
propositions.quote: For example, the interveners Grand Council of the Crees and Cree Regional Authority propose... a distinction be made between three types of Aboriginal and treaty rights: (a) rights that are exclusively collective; (b) rights that are mixed; and (c) rights that are predominantly individual.

propositions.text: Interveners attempt to classify various rights based on these three categories.
propositions.quote: These interveners also attempt to classify a variety of rights on the basis of these three categories.

paragraphs.summary: Interveners propose classifying Aboriginal and treaty rights into three categories and attempt to classify rights accordingly.

propositions.text: Court acknowledges diversity of Aboriginal and treaty rights but declines to develop broad categories at this stage.
propositions.quote: These suggestions bear witness to the diversity of Aboriginal and treaty rights. But I would not... try to develop broad categories for these rights and to slot each right in the appropriate one.

propositions.text: Court acknowledges rights may have collective and individual aspects and entitlements may be created in favour of individuals.
propositions.quote: It will suffice to acknowledge that, despite the critical importance of the collective aspect of Aboriginal and treaty rights, rights may sometimes be assigned to or exercised by individual members of Aboriginal communities, and entitlements may sometimes be created in their favour.

propositions.text: Nothing more need be said about classification at this time.
propositions.quote: Nothing more need be said at this time.

paragraphs.summary: Court acknowledges rights’ diversity and individual aspects but declines broad classification now.

propositions.text: Behns assert Authorizations breach their treaty rights to hunt and trap on traditional family territory within FNFN territory.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, the Behns assert in their defence that the Authorizations are illegal because they breach their treaty rights to hunt and trap... they also allege that specific tracts of land have traditionally been assigned to and associated with particular family groups.

propositions.text: Behns allege Authorizations granted for logging in areas traditionally assigned to them where they exercised hunting and trapping rights.
propositions.quote: They assert in their pleadings that the Authorizations granted to Moulton are for logging in specific areas within the territory traditionally assigned to the Behns, where they have exercised their rights to hunt and trap.

propositions.text: Behns assert they have greater interest in protecting hunting and trapping rights on their traditional family territory than other FNFN members.
propositions.quote: On the basis of an allegation of a connection between their rights to hunt and trap and a specific geographic location within the FNFN territory, the Behns assert that they have a greater interest in the protection of hunting and trapping rights on their traditional family territory than do other members of the FNFN.

propositions.text: It might be argued this connection gives Behns standing to raise violation of their particular rights as defence to tort claim.
propositions.quote: It might be argued that this connection gives them a certain standing to raise the violation of their particular rights as a defence to Moulton’s tort claim.

propositions.text: Final decision on standing unnecessary here because abuse of process issue is determinative.
propositions.quote: But a final decision on this issue of standing is not necessary in this appeal, because another issue will be determinative, that of abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Behns allege Authorizations breach their treaty rights on family territory; standing arguable but abuse of process issue is determinative.

propositions.text: Key issue is whether Behns’ acts constitute abuse of process by raising duty to consult and treaty rights as defence.
propositions.quote: The key issue in this appeal is whether the Behns’ acts constitute an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Raising breach of duty to consult and treaty rights as defence was abuse of process here.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, in the circumstances of this case, raising a breach of the duty to consult and of treaty rights as a defence was an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Behns and FNFN did not legally challenge Authorizations when granted; no judicial review, injunction, or relief sought.
propositions.quote: Neither the Behns nor the FNFN had made any attempt to legally challenge the Authorizations when the British Columbia government granted them. It is common ground that the Behns did not apply for judicial review, ask for an injunction or seek any other form of judicial relief against the province or against Moulton. Nor did the FNFN make any such move.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds raising duty to consult and treaty rights defence was abuse of process; Behns and FNFN did not challenge Authorizations timely.

propositions.text: Clause 9.00 allowed Timber Sales Manager to suspend Authorizations until legal issues resolved if challenged timely.
propositions.quote: Had the Behns acted when the Authorizations were granted, clause 9.00 of the timber sale agreements provided that the Timber Sales Manager had the power to suspend the Authorizations until the legal issues were resolved: trial judgment, at para. 16.

propositions.text: If challenged timely, Moulton would not have believed it was free to plan and start logging operations.
propositions.quote: Moulton would not then have been led to believe that it was free to plan and start its logging operations.

propositions.text: Legal issues like standing could have been addressed at proper time and context if challenged timely.
propositions.quote: Moreover, legal issues like standing could have been addressed at the proper time and in the appropriate context.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes clause allowed suspension of Authorizations if challenged timely; legal issues could have been addressed properly then.

propositions.text: Abuse of process rooted in judge’s inherent discretion to prevent abuse of court’s process; applies beyond criminal law.
propositions.quote: In Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 77, Arbour J. wrote for the majority of this Court that the doctrine of abuse of process has its roots in a judge’s inherent and residual discretion to prevent abuse of the court’s process: para. 35; see also P. M. Perell, “A Survey of Abuse of Process”, in T. L. Archibald and R. S. Echlin, eds., Annual Review of Civil Litigation 2007 (2007), 243.

propositions.text: Abuse of process defined as proceedings unfair to point contrary to justice or oppressive treatment.
propositions.quote: Abuse of process was described in R. v. Power, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 601, at p. 616, as the bringing of proceedings that are “unfair to the point that they are contrary to the interest of justice”, and in R. v. Conway, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1659, at p. 1667, as “oppressive treatment”.

propositions.text: Abuse of process also protects public interest in fair trial and proper administration of justice.
propositions.quote: In addition to proceedings that are oppressive or vexatious and that violate the principles of justice, McLachlin J. (as she then was) said in her dissent in R. v. Scott, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 979, at p. 1007, that the doctrine of abuse of process evokes the “public interest in a fair and just trial process and the proper administration of justice”.

propositions.text: Doctrine applies in various legal contexts, not limited to criminal law.
propositions.quote: Arbour J. observed in C.U.P.E. that the doctrine is not limited to criminal law, but applies in a variety of legal contexts: para. 36.

paragraphs.summary: Prior cases define abuse of process as judge’s discretion to prevent unfair, oppressive proceedings, protecting justice and public interest beyond criminal law.

propositions.text: Abuse of process doctrine is flexible, prevents misuse of court procedure causing unfairness or disrepute to justice.
propositions.quote: The doctrine of abuse of process is characterized by its flexibility. Unlike the concepts of res judicata and issue estoppel, abuse of process is unencumbered by specific requirements. In Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles (2000), 51 O.R. (3d) 481 (C.A.), Goudge J.A., who was dissenting, but whose reasons this Court subsequently approved (2002 SCC 63, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 307), stated at paras. 55-56 that the doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

propositions.text: Abuse of process applies where litigation attempts to relitigate a claim already determined.
propositions.quote: One circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation before the court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim which the court has already determined.

propositions.text: Nordheimer J. found third party claim should be terminated as abuse of process for relitigation.
propositions.quote: See Solomon v. Smith, supra. It is on that basis that Nordheimer J. found that this third party claim ought to be terminated as an abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Abuse of process doctrine is flexible, prevents unfair misuse of court procedure, including relitigation of claims already decided.

propositions.text: The doctrine of abuse of process centers on administration of justice and fairness.
propositions.quote: the administration of justice and fairness are at the heart of the doctrine of abuse of process

propositions.text: In Canam Enterprises and C.U.P.E., abuse of process precluded relitigation when issue estoppel requirements were unmet.
propositions.quote: In Canam Enterprises and in C.U.P.E., the doctrine was used to preclude relitigation of an issue in circumstances in which the requirements for issue estoppel were not met

propositions.text: Abuse of process is not limited to preventing relitigation.
propositions.quote: But it is not limited to preventing relitigation

propositions.text: In Blencoe, unreasonable delay causing serious prejudice can be abuse of process.
propositions.quote: in Blencoe v. British Columbia (Human Rights Commission), 2000 SCC 44, [2000] 2 S.C.R. 307, the Court held that an unreasonable delay that causes serious prejudice could amount to an abuse of process

propositions.text: Abuse of process doctrine is flexible to protect administration of justice's reputation.
propositions.quote: The doctrine of abuse of process is flexible, and it exists to ensure that the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute

paragraphs.summary: The court explains abuse of process doctrine centers on justice and fairness, citing Canam, C.U.P.E., and Blencoe cases, emphasizing its flexibility.

propositions.text: The Behns' acts constitute abuse of process.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, the Behns’ acts amount to an abuse of process

propositions.text: The Behns objected to Authorizations as infringing treaty rights and breaching duty to consult.
propositions.quote: The Behns clearly objected to the validity of the Authorizations on the grounds that the Authorizations infringed their treaty rights and that the Crown had breached its duty to consult

propositions.text: The Behns now claim standing to raise these issues.
propositions.quote: whereas they now claim to have standing to raise these issues

propositions.text: The Behns did not seek to resolve standing or contest Authorizations legally when issued.
propositions.quote: the Behns did not seek to resolve the issue of standing, nor did they contest the validity of the Authorizations by legal means when they were issued

propositions.text: The Behns did not raise concerns with Moulton after Authorizations were issued.
propositions.quote: They did not raise their concerns with Moulton after the Authorizations were issued

propositions.text: The Behns set up a camp blocking access to Moulton's logging sites without warning.
propositions.quote: Instead, without any warning, they set up a camp that blocked access to the logging sites assigned to Moulton

propositions.text: Behns forced Moulton to choose court or forgo timber harvesting after incurring costs.
propositions.quote: By doing so, the Behns put Moulton in the position of having either to go to court or to forgo harvesting timber pursuant to the Authorizations it had received after having incurred substantial costs to start its operations

propositions.text: Allowing Behns to raise treaty rights and duty to consult defense now would condone self-help and harm justice administration.
propositions.quote: To allow the Behns to raise their defence based on treaty rights and on a breach of the duty to consult at this point would be tantamount to condoning self-help remedies and would bring the administration of justice into disrepute

propositions.text: Allowing this defense repudiates mutual good faith in Crown's constitutional duty to consult First Nations.
propositions.quote: It would also amount to a repudiation of the duty of mutual good faith that animates the discharge of the Crown’s constitutional duty to consult First Nations

propositions.text: Doctrine of abuse of process applies; appellants cannot raise treaty rights and duty to consult breach as defense.
propositions.quote: The doctrine of abuse of process applies, and the appellants cannot raise a breach of their treaty rights and of the duty to consult as a defence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Behns abused process by blocking access without legal challenge, barring their treaty rights and duty to consult defense now.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs to respondent Moulton.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs to the respondent Moulton. Appeal dismissed with costs

propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellants: Janes Freedman Kyle Law Corporation, Vancouver. Solicitors for the respondent Moulton Contracting Ltd.: Fasken Martineau DuMoulin, Vancouver.
